main_message: Steel power used to mean owning the cheapest route from ore and coal to rail (Carnegie). Today governments (tariffs, quotas, a golden share) and carbon pricing (CBAM) decide who gets access to that route and on what terms. Steel matters as a share and as control, not just as tonnage.
why_hook: 88M tonnes then versus 82M now, but only 4% of the world, and then 'guarded like a weapon'. It's a clean paradox with a concrete question. It's a bit stat-heavy, but the question is a good one.
what_connects_layers: The 'path' metaphor: who controls the route from rock to rail, and who sets the toll. It works for Carnegie and for the golden share. The carbon part is a stretch, because a carbon price is a different kind of thing from owning a supply chain, so the link feels stitched on. The 'one machine' promise in the intro is bigger than what the ending delivers.
ending_comment: It does answer it: 'share and control of the path, not tonnage'. Then it hedges with 'whether that is worth what it costs, numbers can't settle'. That lets the video off the hook on whether the tariffs actually work. The Braddock closing image is nice but doesn't add much.

boring_or_slow.why: Ton-by-ton logistics with lots of miles and tonnages. It gets dry before the point lands.
A tariff timeline with many dates (2018, Feb 2025, June 2025, April 2026, June 2026). It reads like a legal log.
Heavy on numbers: CO2 intensities, euro prices, free allowances and caveats. Hard to follow by ear.
Carnegie biography and land prices per acre. Slow, and not obviously needed.

confusing.why: Is CBAM actually costing importers 190 euros a tonne, or not? The 'illustration only' framing muddies how much it really matters.

confusing.quote: A drop of about seven percent. Not zero.
confusing.why: It says output is down 7% and the share fell to 4%. Elsewhere the line says the industry 'fell by half' and came back. Which is it: dying or fine?
The 'machine' is never defined up front. It only becomes 'path and toll' at the end.
The consent rights are described but the full agreement is secret, so I can't tell how much control Washington really has.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: a cost no price list shows
felt_biased_or_one_sided.direction: sympathetic to workers / critical of Carnegie
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: An editorial aside inserted into a neutral fact chain. The sentence about Homestead is where the narrator's voice leans.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: fifteen times as much in subsidies
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: Only Chinese overcapacity and exports are highlighted. Little about US or EU subsidies, or why China built that capacity. The OECD is presented as neutral, which a skeptic may question.
It uses the administration's own 77% vs 80% figure to suggest the tariffs fall short, and cites a study on the 2002 tariffs hurting users. It's thin on the other side's case, like jobs or investment.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: sorts it mainly by how it was made
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: CBAM is presented as the smarter tool without noting complaints from trade partners or its protectionist side.

claims_you_doubt.why: The 1950 share was inflated by a war-wrecked world. That is plausible, but it's an opinion stated as a fact, with no evidence given.
Sweeping claim from one anecdote (Carnegie's own autobiography, which is self-serving). Steel pricing is also shaped by demand, technology and policy.

claims_you_doubt.quote: the White House said it intervened
claims_you_doubt.why: The golden share story rests on company press releases and the White House's own framing. I'd want independent confirmation of what really happened.

claims_you_doubt.quote: Washington treats it as a security question
claims_you_doubt.why: Tariffs are presented as a security move, but could just as well be lobbying and industry protection. The video doesn't test that motive.

claims_you_doubt.quote: a country can import its phones and still function
claims_you_doubt.why: A confident claim with no source. Plenty of countries import steel and function fine, including most of Europe.

best_moment: 06: It puts the 'dying industry' myth next to the numbers (down about 7%, not zero) and explains the share drop by the world growing about ten times. It's the one part that really rebuts the lazy narrative and shows the sources.
top3_fixes: Define the 'machine' (path plus toll) in the intro in one plain sentence, and cut the opening promise to 'judge whether we're right', because the ending doesn't give a test for that.
Cut the numbers in 03, 07 and 10 by about a third. Keep one headline figure per segment (for example, 4 tons of material per ton of steel, 25% to 50%, 190 vs 57 euros) and give the rest on screen.

Give the other side more space: why countries distrust cheap imports versus why tariffs raise costs for steel users, and who benefits (incumbent producers, unions) from the 'national security' framing. Also say plainly what the evidence says about whether the tariffs worked.
